name: authorization-enforcer
intent: Centralise authorization as a policy decision and enforce it at one complete-mediation point in the request or invocation pipeline, so every protected access uses the same trusted subject/action/resource input and policy changes do not require edits in the handlers they protect.
problem: Authorization rules are scattered through controllers, services and handlers: each call site interprets roles or attributes differently, duplicates decisions, and leaves forgotten routes open. A policy change then requires a hunt through entry points, while object-level and internal service calls can bypass a coarse check entirely; the system needs one auditable decision contract plus an enforcement point that every protected path actually traverses.
context: Request- and invocation-oriented tiers - web APIs, RPC services, message dispatchers, scheduled jobs and method calls - where authorization can be expressed from a trusted subject, action and resource, and where the host provides a boundary hook (servlet filter, middleware, guard, action function, dispatcher or AOP interceptor). An authenticated principal must already be available from the security context (see Authenticator, Security Context and Authentication Enforcer); the pattern owns authorization and enforcement, not identity proof, transport isolation or a single object's invariant. If the boundary lacks resource attributes, combine it with a resource-level check rather than treating coarse mediation as complete.
benefits: One decision point: rules live in a single evaluator, so changing a policy, reviewing it or auditing it touches one place instead of every handler.
Consistent enforcement: every request passes the same interception point, which removes the 'forgot the check' class of holes once the point is wired at the boundary with a deny-by-default fallback.
Separation of concerns: handlers keep doing the operation, the evaluator keeps deciding who may do it, and the two evolve independently.
Testability: the decision is a pure function of subject, action and resource, so the policy matrix can be tested without HTTP, and enforcement is exercised once at the boundary.

Pluggable policy models: RBAC, ABAC or relationship rules can replace each other behind the same decision interface, and an external PDP (OPA, Casbin, an authorization service) can take over without touching call sites.

Centralised failure handling and audit: denials become a uniform 401/403 and the decision itself can be logged (subject, action, resource, outcome), which is what incident response and compliance reviews ask for.
tradeoffs: The central decision point is a chokepoint: an extra dependency on every protected request (latency, availability) that has to be designed to fail closed, and one misconfiguration now affects every path at once.

Its failure mode is silent: any route, service call or background job that is not wired through the enforcement point looks protected but is not, so 'centralised' has to be verified rather than assumed.

Policy drift and context starvation: rules held apart from the resource they protect can diverge from domain invariants, and boundary-level decisions often lack the resource attributes that only exist deeper in the call chain - pushing resource checks back into business code, where scattering returns.
Administration cost: role or attribute explosion, a policy store to operate, cache invalidation when permissions change, and audit trails to retain.
Legibility: annotation- or config-driven authorization hides the rules from the handler that is being protected, so a missing rule silently allows unless deny-by-default is explicit everywhere.
A broader test surface: the combination of policy, resource and identity has to be covered, and every request pays for a decision that previous inline checks sometimes avoided.

participants.responsibility: The single interception point in front of protected operations (filter, middleware, guard, action function, AOP interceptor): it obtains a decision for the request and allows or denies, but never evaluates rules itself.
Evaluates the policy for the subject, action and resource and returns a decision; the only place where authorization rules live, ideally free of I/O so it is unit-testable.
Holds the rules and the attributes they reference - role assignments, resource attributes, policy files or database, or an external PDP service - and supplies them to the decision point.
The management surface where operators define and publish policies to the PDP. Separating PAP from PDP allows policy changes without redeploying the decision engine.
The authenticated identity with its roles and attributes, supplied by the security context; the enforcer consumes the subject, it never authenticates one.
The target of the request and the operation attempted (URL plus method, service method plus arguments, message plus operation); together with the subject they form the decision input.
Turns a denial into the uniform response (401/403 without leaking internals) and records the decision for monitoring and audit; centralised so every path fails the same way.

use_cases: HTTP APIs where endpoint groups require roles or scopes and every request must be authorised before the controller body runs.
Method-level business operations (approve an invoice, refund a payment) whose decision depends on the arguments or the loaded aggregate, enforced by an interception proxy around the service bean.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant isolation is a policy applied uniformly at the boundary and re-checked for object access, so no query path can cross tenants.
Microservices delegating the decision to a central PDP or policy service (policy sidecar, Casbin-backed service) while each service keeps its own local enforcement point.
APIs published through a gateway that denies by default at the edge and forwards the subject context to downstream services for their own enforcement.
Regulated systems that must record every access decision and handle denials uniformly, including the case where policy changes must be applied without redeploying the protected code.
Kubernetes admission control where the API server acts as PEP and an OPA/Gatekeeper instance acts as PDP evaluating resource shape before objects are persisted.
AI agent tool governance where an MCP gateway intercepts tool calls and enforces policy (allow/deny/escalate) before the agent can invoke enterprise tools.
Zero-trust perimeters where every east-west service-to-service hop is re-authorized via a service mesh sidecar (Envoy ext_authz) rather than trusting the internal network.
Regulated workloads (HIPAA, PCI-DSS) requiring decision logs with masked PII, where an EOPA sidecar redacts before shipping to a SIEM.
Spring Security's AuthorizationManager behind AuthorizationFilter, using ordered request matchers and anyRequest().denyAll() to make a web application an explicit allow list.

ASP.NET Core policy-based authorization, where named policies and IAuthorizationHandler instances are applied by [Authorize]/RequireAuthorization and a fallback policy protects endpoints with no metadata.
An OPA sidecar queried by a service-local policy enforcement point, or an XACML PEP/PDP/PIP deployment, where policy decisions are externalised but the protected service still enforces every request.
avoid_when: The request has no trusted principal yet: use Authentication Enforcer first, because this pattern authorizes an already authenticated subject and must not become an identity-verification substitute.
There is one entry point and one static rule: use a local Guard Clause or Policy Guard, because an interceptor plus policy store obscures a rule that has no reuse or change pressure.

The requirement is an invariant of one object (for example, only its owner may mutate it) or needs attributes loaded deep in the operation: use a domain guard/resource-level check alongside or instead of the boundary enforcer, because a URL-only decision cannot prevent object-level gaps.

The goal is to isolate or mediate an entire backend rather than decide subject/action/resource access: use a Secure Proxy for that transport or boundary mediation, because an authorization enforcer does not replace network or protocol isolation.
anti_patterns: Scattered inline checks (if (user.isAdmin()), hasRole(...) in controllers and services) -> rule copies diverge and a missed call site stays open -> centralize the decision in the PDP and enforce it at the boundary.
Client-side or UI-only enforcement -> users can call the API directly or tamper with the page -> enforce on trusted server-side requests and use UI checks only as presentation.
Gateway-only enforcement -> internal service-to-service, worker or message paths bypass the perimeter -> add PEPs at every service boundary that owns protected data.
Deciding from unverified headers, parameters or self-asserted claims -> the subject can widen its own permissions -> build input from a validated security context and server-side attributes.
Default-allow configuration -> an unlisted endpoint is reachable until someone notices -> use an explicit deny-by-default fallback and an integration check for coverage.

Swallowing the denial (logging it, redirecting without a 403, or continuing after AccessDeniedException) -> the forbidden operation still executes or becomes indistinguishable from success -> stop the pipeline and return the framework's denial response.
Checking only the record identifier or URL -> parameter tampering permits BOLA/IDOR or cross-tenant access -> authorize the loaded resource and tenant, then enforce the domain invariant.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the decision (what is allowed) is kept apart from the enforcement (stopping the request).
Single responsibility: one enforcement point and one decision point; handlers own neither.
Fail-safe defaults: an unmatched rule, a missing policy or an error in the decision denies access.
Complete mediation: every access to a protected resource passes the enforcement point, not just the first one.
Least privilege: rules grant the minimum required, and the subject's authorities are derived from roles and attributes rather than trusted from the caller.
Open/closed and dependency inversion: new policies and subjects arrive without editing handlers, and the enforcement point depends on an abstract decision interface (or an external PDP).
Defence in depth: gateway, mesh, and in-app enforcement layers are complementary - one layer alone is not complete mediation.
best_practices: Centralise the decision in one evaluator and keep every rule there; handlers ask for a decision, they never make one.
Deny by default: add a catch-all rule (denyAll, fallback policy, deny when no metadata is present) so new endpoints are protected until explicitly opened.
Evaluate on every request with trusted inputs: subject attributes from the security context or session, never from client-supplied claims alone.
Keep enforcement at the boundary and add defence in depth where sensitive operations also need resource-level checks - one layer is not automatically complete mediation.
Handle denials in one place: map to 401/403 without leaking internals, and log the decision (subject, action, resource, outcome) for monitoring and audit.
Treat the decision point as a dependency: bound its latency, cache only safe results with explicit invalidation on permission changes, and fail closed when it is unavailable.
Test the policy matrix (allow and deny per role, attribute and resource) and include a test proving that an unguarded route is rejected by the fallback rule.
Verify complete mediation with integration tests: assert that every registered route passes through the enforcement point, and that a bare request to an unwired path is denied.
Keep the PDP stateless and pure: policy state belongs in the policy store, not in PDP process memory - this makes horizontal scaling straightforward.
Keep the PAP (Policy Administration Point) out-of-band from the PDP: policy authors publish reviewed, signed bundles or updates at runtime so policy changes do not require an application deploy.
Align input shape consistently across all PEPs: every enforcement point must construct the same subject/action/resource document so decision logs are replayable and auditable.
Use OPA partial evaluation or Cedar schema validation to catch policy syntax errors before they reach production bundles.
In multi-tenant systems, include tenant context in the PDP input document and verify tenant isolation at the PEP before forwarding to the PDP.
Scope PDP cache TTLs tightly for high-privilege roles; consider caching only the coarse RBAC gate while evaluating ABAC policies per request.
sources: Nagappan, Steel & Lai, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management (2005) - the Authorization Enforcer pattern (Web Tier patterns), described as how authorization should be enforced after user authentication, related to Intercepting Filter and Context Object.

Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering (2005) - the Authorization pattern and its enforcement-point responsibilities.
https://coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com/patterns.htm
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html

OWASP Top 10 A01:2021 Broken Access Control - the canonical enumeration of access-control failure classes that this pattern prevents, including BOLA/IDOR, privilege escalation, and missing enforcement.
NIST CSRC - Authorization (csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/authorization) - standard federal definition of authorization as a decision preceding enforcement.
NIST SP 800-162 - Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) - defines the PDP, PEP, PIP and PAP roles and their interactions for attribute-based authorization systems.
NISTIR 7987 - Policy Machine: Features, Architecture, and Specification - a policy-neutral framework that formalises the reference monitor concept and shows how RBAC, ABAC and other models map to it.

Anderson, J.P. (1972). Computer Security Technology Planning Study (Air Force report, ESD-TR-73-51) - the original Anderson Report that introduced the Reference Monitor concept with its three requirements: complete mediation, tamperproof, and verifiability.

Schneider, F.B. (1999). Enforceable Security Policies (Cornell CS) - formal characterisation of the EM (Execution Monitoring) class of enforcement mechanisms including reference monitors; proves what policies are enforceable and what cannot be caught by runtime monitoring alone.

Elrakaiby & Le Traon (2012). A PEP-PDP Architecture to Monitor and Enforce Security Policies in Java Applications (University of Luxembourg) - demonstrates automated PEP generation using AOP for Java, with a stateful PDP backed by Drools; shows that separating enforcement from decision scales to runtime policy update.
XACML v3.0 Core Specification (OASIS, 2003 and revisions) - the canonical standard defining PEP/PDP/PIP/PAP architecture; still the de-facto reference model for authorization frameworks.

OpenID AuthZen Authorization Design Patterns (github.com/openid/authzen) - compares five architectural patterns for authorization (Traditional PEP/PDP, Provisioning, External API Call, User Journey, Authorization Mesh) with suitability matrices for COTS, GraphQL, API Gateways and microservices.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance - Using OPA for SaaS Multitenant API Access Authorization (docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance) - documents centralized PDP with PEPs on APIs as industry best practice; covers OPA sidecar, distributed PDP, and embedded SDK deployment patterns with latency and availability trade-offs.

Permit.io blog - Stop Rebuilding Permissions in Application Code (2026) - practitioner account of five authorization rewrites at a SaaS company; describes role explosion, policy velocity, and hybrid PDP architectures using OPAL for policy push.

Lorikeet Security - RBAC vs ABAC: Choosing the Right Access Control Model (2026) - common access-control implementation mistakes found in code reviews: frontend-only checks, missing object-level authorization, inconsistent enforcement, hardcoded role checks, privilege escalation through parameter manipulation, tenant isolation failures.

SessionManager.com - Policy Enforcement Points in Microservices and Choosing Between RBAC and ABAC (2026) - detailed treatment of PEP placement (API gateway, service mesh sidecar, in-app middleware), the three threats that dominate (fail-open, client-claim trust, edge-only enforcement), and the RBAC/ABAC decision matrix.

EnforceAuth Documentation (docs.enforceauth.com) - reference architectures for Kubernetes sidecar PDP, centralized PDP for polyglot fleets, regulated workloads with EOPA masking, AI agent/MCP tool governance via MCP Authorization Gateway, and Kubernetes cluster admission (OPA Gatekeeper).

KasperskyOS PDP Pattern Documentation (support.kaspersky.ru) - policy decision point encapsulation pattern; emphasises that verification-time vs usage-time drift is a critical design concern when policy depends on rapidly-changing resource state.

Cornell CS FBS - Reference Monitors (coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com) - authoritative treatment of the reference monitor and complete mediation; connects the three Anderson requirements to modern distributed enforcement architectures.

Heckman (2015). Every Secure System Wants to Be a Reference Monitor (ISSA Journal) - argues that the reference monitor concept is the unifying framework for security design and that every modern compromise violates at least one of the three properties (completeness, isolation, verifiability).

NPS Calhoun - Reference Monitor Concept (nps.edu/calhoun) - educational treatment of the Reference Monitor Concept from its 1972 Anderson origin through modern distributed implementations; covers hardware virtualisation for complete mediation and the gap between reference monitor ideal and production reality.

Codelit.io - RBAC vs ABAC: A Complete Guide to Access Control Models - practical implementation guide covering Kubernetes RBAC best practices, middleware enforcement, per-resource checks, and the hybrid RBAC+ABAC model; emphasises that policy engines (OPA, Cedar, Casbin) externalise authorization logic.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) documentation - Rego policy language reference and deployment guides covering bundle polling, decision logging, partial evaluation, and the fail-closed PEP contract.

related_patterns_notes.authentication-enforcer: establishes and validates the principal; Authorization Enforcer consumes that trusted identity to decide access.
related_patterns_notes.security-context: carries the authenticated subject and its attributes; Authorization Enforcer reads it but does not populate or authenticate it.
related_patterns_notes.subject-descriptor: defines the subject's roles, claims or attributes; Authorization Enforcer uses that descriptor as decision input.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: supplies generic invocation wrapping; Authorization Enforcer specializes the boundary with a policy decision and deny behavior.
related_patterns_notes.policy-guard: applies a focused policy predicate around one operation; Authorization Enforcer centralizes reusable decisions across a complete boundary.
related_patterns_notes.reference-monitor: states the ideal of complete, tamper-resistant and verifiable mediation; Authorization Enforcer is one practical application at service boundaries.
related_patterns_notes.complete-mediation: requires every access to be checked; Authorization Enforcer provides the PEP/PDP structure, but wiring still has to prove coverage.
related_patterns_notes.secure-base-action: coordinates web-tier security concerns in a shared action base; Authorization Enforcer is the authorization decision/enforcement concern it may delegate.
related_patterns_notes.zanzibar: provides a relationship-based authorization model and tuple graph; Authorization Enforcer is the enforcement boundary that can call such a model.
related_patterns_notes.rebac: describes relationship-based policy semantics; Authorization Enforcer describes where the resulting decision is applied.
